A baby has died of hypothermia in southern Gaza, amid plummeting temperatures and continuing Israeli restrictions on aid, AFP reported, citing medical sources.
Nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq was found dead by his father as they sheltered in a tent in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis overnight.
Raqiq’s father Ahmed, stood weeping outside Nasser Hospital, as he held his son’s shrouded body.
“I woke up only to see his skin had turned blue so I rushed him to Nasser Hospital, but he had already died from hypothermia and frozen to death,” he told AFP.
“I am in complete shock. I found myself holding my son wrapped in a burial shroud.”
Heavy rains have swept through Gaza, inundating thousands of tents where the majority of the enclave’s population are forced to shelter amid ongoing Israeli restrictions on aid entering the territory.
As temperatures plummeted on Thursday, Israeli attacks across Gaza surged, with health officials putting the total toll of people killed since dawn at 11.
The day before baby Raqiq’s death, two Israeli drones tore through that same hospital’s surgical department, killing six people, including a surgeon and a child and wounding around 30 others.
An AFP journalist who was at the scene reported that one of the building's exterior staircases had partially collapsed and that indoors an entire floor was damaged, with broken concrete from collapsed walls mixed with broken medical equipment.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UN rights chief demands Houthis return body of staff member who died in custody
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
UN rights chief demands Houthis return body of staff member who died in custody
The UN's human rights chief on Friday demanded the return of the body of a Yemeni staff member who died of unknown causes weeks ago, after more than two years in Houthi custody.
Mohammed al-Shami's family learned of his death on 30 October, more than a month after it happened, and has received no explanation of the cause or circumstances.
The Houthis had held Shami since 6 June 2024.
"Our colleague must be laid to rest in a dignified manner, in accordance with the wishes of his family - which was denied contact with him for two years while he was in detention," said Volker Turk, the UN high commissioner for human rights.
In a statement earlier this week, Shami's family said the Houthis had agreed in principle to an investigation.
"Do not allow Mohammed to die twice: once when he was taken from his family and disappeared, and again when the truth about his fate is allowed to disappear from the world," the statement said.
More than 70 UN employees and dozens of humanitarian workers remain in detention in Yemen.
Turk's office said a video circulating this week appeared to show one of them "confessing" and voiced fears that the detainees may be subjected to torture or ill-treatment.
#Yemen: @volker_turk demands that the body of Mohammed Al-Shami, colleague deceased in Houthi custody, be returned to his family without delay, and that the Houthi de facto authorities take urgent steps to establish the date, cause and circumstances of his death, and to ensure those responsible are held accountable. Türk calls for all detained @UN and humanitarian personnel to be released immediately and unconditionally. The Houthi de facto authorities must immediately provide information on the whereabouts and health of all detainees. https://t.co/y8EJthxBa0
— UN Human Rights (@UNHumanRights) November 13, 2026

Leaflets at the event promoted medical clinics in settlements in occupied Palestinian territory, which the British government considers illegal in line with international law, Sky News reported.
Distributed by the Israeli healthcare provider Terem, the leaflets advertised vacancies in clinics in the West Bank settlements of Ma'ale Adumim, Beitar Illit and Modiin Illit, as well as Katzrin in the Golan Heights, which Britain recognises as occupied Syrian territory.

data.title: Middle East Eye: France calls for more pressure on Houthis to end attacks on Saudi Arabia
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
France calls for more pressure on Houthis to end attacks on Saudi Arabia
France called for greater pressure on Yemen's Houthis to end their attacks in the region, particularly against Saudi Arabia.
"Our position is that it is necessary to increase pressure on the Houthis so that they put an end to their unacceptable attacks and provocations, particularly against Saudi territory, but not only there," spokesperson for the French foreign ministry Pascal Confavreux told a news conference on Friday.
He was responding to a question on whether Paris backed the idea of the European Union designating the Houthis as a terrorist organisation.
Saudi Arabia is pressing the EU to make the designation, but has yet to overcome European concerns that it could undermine a future peace process, Reuters reported, citing six European officials.
Also on Thursday, the UN Security Council voted unanimously to extend Yemen-related sanctions, including asset freezes and travel bans, for another year, while demanding an end to the group's attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) welcomed the resolution on Friday.
"This resolution represents a significant step in consolidating the international stance that rejects the treacherous Houthi attacks," GCC Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said in a statement.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump says Saudi Arabia is 'disintegrating'
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Trump says Saudi Arabia is 'disintegrating'
Saudi Arabia is “disintegrating”, US President Donald Trump said in an interview released on Friday, which is likely to offend the kingdom, as it suffers missile and drone strikes from Yemen’s Houthis.
Trump passed judgment on Saudi Arabia, one of the US’s closest allies, in an interview with Stephen A Smith, boasting he could destroy Iran in three days by attacking civilian infrastructure but that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states have asked him not to because of their own weaknesses.
“If I want to take them out, I hit their [energy] in one day. Their energy is gone. In one day, their bridges are gone, and in one day, their manufacturing capability is gone. It would only take me three days, one day each,” Trump said.
"Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while because they're disintegrating," Trump said.
"Qatar, if you look at that, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, all of them would much prefer the waiting period,” he added.
This is not the first time Trump has appeared to enjoy bragging about the leverage he has over Gulf states and, particularly, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Saudi Arabia has relied on the US as its security guarantor since WWII.
“He (MBS) didn’t think this was going to happen… he didn’t think he’d be kissing my ass… he thought it’d be just another American president that was a loser… but now he has to be nice to me,” Trump said in March, when the war on Iran was in full swing.

data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
New Turkey-Qatar pact pledges joint stance against external attacks
Turkey and Qatar have pledged a unified stance against any external armed attack on either country, according to a joint statement issued after they signed the defence agreement.
The statement said the pact aims to strengthen collective defence and promote regional security.
Under it, the two countries will consult on threats to their security, regional and global security issues, and defence policy.
They will also expand cooperation through joint military exercises, defence industry projects and personnel training exchanges.
The statement added that the agreement reflects both countries’ commitment to safeguarding their sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as their shared vision of a more secure and stable regional order.
The two sides also said they were ready to pursue energy cooperation, particularly in liquefied natural gas trade.

The encounters have prompted questions about the purpose of his trip, as he held high-level meetings in Beirut during a time of heightened tensions in the region.
Some in the Middle East regard him as a potential successor to his father. But sources close to Erdogan told MEE that the visit was one of many trips he has made across the region and beyond in recent years, and carries no political significance.
Erdogan was in Tokyo earlier this month and also visited Syria earlier this year. He also travels to Europe, North Africa and South Asia on trips he arranges independently.

People walk through Terminal 7 at JFK Airport in New York City, on 29 August 2025 (Michael M Santiago/Getty Images via AFP)

Activists, joined by New York State Senator Jabari Brisport, gathered outside the World Trade Center on Thursday, protesting against the transportation of military-related materials through JFK International Airport (JFK).
The protest, organised under the “Break the Chain” campaign led by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), comes amid reporting from The Intercept that Challenge Airlines cargo flights have transported materials including nitrocellulose, bomb casings and guidance kits from JFK to Israel.
Open-source data documented in the report reveals weapons flown out of JFK are tied to mass casualty attacks in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran.
Challenge Airlines is an Israel-based cargo airline and logistics company founded in 1976.
The Intercept reported that thousands of pounds worth of parts for "bunker-buster" bombs went through JFK during the height of the US-Israeli war on Iran. The war began on 28 February.
Break the Chain says that military cargo bound for Israel passes through JFK Airport regularly, sometimes multiple times a week, and that civilian infrastructure should not be used for the benefit of the Israeli military.
Protesters, including members of Jewish Voice for Peace, Palestinian Youth Movement, Democratic Socialists of America, and Brooklyn for Peace called for an end to the shipments and greater accountability from the Port Authority, which has jurisdiction over JFK Airport.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Two tankers hit sea mines in Hormuz: IRGC
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Two tankers hit sea mines in Hormuz: IRGC
Two oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said, according to Iranian state TV.
The tankers had been trying to cross the strait without coordinating with Iranian authorities, it said, without giving further details.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Houthis say they attacked Riyadh airport and Saudi oil pipeline
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Houthis say they attacked Riyadh airport and Saudi oil pipeline
Yemen's Houthis said they attacked Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which carries crude oil to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted the airport with a drone, and a pumping station east of Riyadh with two drones.
The group also fired two ballistic missiles at what Saree described as Saudi troop concentrations in the al-Tuwal area of Jazan, in southern Saudi Arabia, he said.
The group's statements came hours after Saudi civil defence issued an all-clear for the province, which is home to a Saudi Aramco refinery with a capacity of 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.
Inside Yemen, Saree said the Houthis struck Saudi weapons depots at the Ras Abbas camp in Aden with ballistic missiles and drones.
He added that they also fired missiles at forces under the command of Saudi officers in Lahj and al-Jawf provinces, claiming they caused many casualties.
Saudi Arabia did not immediately confirm the Houthi claims.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli forces detain Palestinian groom in wedding raid as settler attacks continue across West Bank
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Israeli forces detain Palestinian groom in wedding raid as settler attacks continue across West Bank
Israeli forces and settlers carried out a series of attacks across the occupied West Bank on Friday, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
In Jaba’, south of Jenin, Israeli forces stormed the town, firing live ammunition and tear gas, and shot a young Palestinian man in the thigh, the Palestinian Red Crescent Society said.
Near Ramallah, Israeli forces raided a wedding hall in the village of al-Mughayyir, firing tear gas at around 150 guests and detaining four people, including the groom, Wafa said, citing Palestinian residents.
In the same village, troops stormed the home of Palestinian man, Hamed Abu Naim, seized keys and forced the family out.
In Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, several Palestinians were treated for tear gas inhalation after Israeli forces fired tear gas at residents and their homes.
According to residents, troops had entered the town to protect Israeli settlers who had chased children near its entrance and tried to assault them. Soldiers also stopped a vehicle at the entrance and beat its driver.
South of Yatta, in the Hebron governorate, settlers besieged the home of Yousef Shannaran for the 40th consecutive day, media activist Osama Makhamra told Wafa.
He said settlers had put back up a tent next to the house that Israeli forces had previously removed, so the family can only come and go by coordinating with nearby troops. Settlers also threw stones at the home, smashed its windows and doors and poisoned the family’s water well, he added.
Near Khirbet Srouj, west of Jenin, settlers attacked Palestinian families harvesting olives and stole harvested olives and equipment.
In occupied East Jerusalem, two Palestinian brothers were forced to demolish their own homes in Sur Baher after the Israeli municipality said they had been built without permits.
Israeli forces also detained a Palestinian child and a woman in the southern Hebron area, Quds News

data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump extends shipping law waiver for 90 days amid Iran war fuel price rise
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Trump extends shipping law waiver for 90 days amid Iran war fuel price rise
US President Donald Trump has extended by 90 days a waiver of a shipping law so that foreign-flagged ships can transport oil and other commodities between US ports, a White House official said on Friday.
The administration would extend the waiver of the more than 100-year-old Jones Act, Reuters reported, citing industry sources.
The administration issued a blanket waiver in March, a month after the US launched its war on Iran, in an effort to lower oil and fuel prices.
When it extended the waiver in August, it said it would decide cases on a case-by-case basis, a condition that also applies to the latest extension.
The Jones Act requires cargo moving between US ports to be carried on ships built in the US, owned by US companies, and crewed by American workers. The waiver aims to lower gasoline, diesel, and fertiliser prices, which have risen because of the war.
Since March, an additional 90 million barrels of petroleum, mostly refined products, have been shipped between US ports under the waiver, the White House said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Six Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes across Gaza
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Six Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes across Gaza
Israeli attacks killed six Palestinians and injured around 20 others across the Gaza Strip on Friday, according to medical sources and witnesses.
In Deir al-Balah, a double-tap strike hit civilians who were helping victims of an earlier attack, witnesses said.
Israeli artillery shelled the area around the al-Qastal Towers residential complex, east of the city, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported. Those wounded were taken to al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir al-Balah.
Israeli artillery also shelled eastern areas of Gaza City, Wafa added.
Since the ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025, Israeli attacks have killed 1,622 Palestinians and injured 5,878 others, according to Gaza's health ministry.

data.title: Middle East Eye: US responds to suspected drone activity over UK air base used in Iran strikes
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
US responds to suspected drone activity over UK air base used in Iran strikes
US Air Force personnel at the RAF Lakenheath base in Britain responded to “suspected unauthorised drone activity” on Friday evening, a US Air Force spokesperson said, adding that no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected.
“We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, US and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families,” the spokesperson said by email.
Britain's Ministry of Defence said US Air Force Security Forces personnel had responded to reports of unauthorised drone activity and that the situation had been resolved.
In recent weeks, the US has moved bombers that had been used to strike Iran out of Britain, and relocated large refuelling aircraft from Britain to Germany. The Wall Street Journal reported that the moves were due to a threat from Iran.
The bombers left RAF Fairford on security grounds after a group of men approached the base in white vans on the night of 27 September.
Two men were charged last month in relation to that incident, with prosecutors alleging that one of them had tried to assist Iranian intelligence in Britain.
The US Justice Department said this week that a member of an Iran-backed militia had plotted to attack the Fairford base while detained in the US on criminal charges.
Tehran has denied involvement in the Fairford incident and rejected other accusations of malign activity in Britain.
